items.prompt: What is a principle, in this unit's sense?
choices: Whatever you feel most strongly about right now
Any rule that appears in the team handbook
A line that, if crossed, changes what you will tolerate
items.explanation: A principle is about what crossing it changes, not about intensity or paperwork.

items.prompt: Two workable naming conventions: one teammate prefers each. Principle or preference?
choices: Preference, since both ways work fine
Principle, since you feel strongly about it
Principle, since it affects the whole team
items.explanation: Both options work, so it is a preference.

items.prompt: Which is a reliable guide to whether a fight is worth having?
choices: How loudly the other person objects
What is actually at stake in it
How well-connected the other person is
items.explanation: Stakes decide it; volume and connections do not.

items.prompt: What goes wrong if you fight every battle?
choices: You lose the ability to read any room
Your principles become easier to negotiate
People stop taking your objections seriously
items.explanation: Constant objecting devalues the objections, including the important ones.

items.prompt: What goes wrong if you fight none?
choices: Your objections get taken too seriously
You slowly erode what you reliably stand on
You burn out from the sheer number of fights
items.explanation: Enough 'not worth it this time' leaves nothing you stand on.

items.prompt: Which of these is a preference?
choices: Your proposal lost to a sound alternative
A design that will charge customers twice
A plan that would hide a known safety gap
items.explanation: The outcome is fine; only your ego took the hit.

items.prompt: What happens if you treat a preference as sacred?
choices: You become too flexible about real harm
You stop being asked for any opinion
You waste credibility on trivial fights
items.explanation: Fighting over preferences wears down the credibility you need later.

items.prompt: Which question helps separate principle from preference?
choices: Would I win if I pushed hard enough here?
Would crossing it change what I tolerate?
Would the other person be upset by my view?
items.explanation: The first question asks about the line itself, not the outcome of the argument.

items.prompt: Two reviewers are equally insistent. One wants a helper renamed, though either name works. The other wants to skip a check that prevents duplicate charges. What fits the split?
choices: Yield on the name; push on the missing check
Treat both alike, since insistence signals weight
Push on both, since small things add up
Yield on both, since neither reviewer will back down
items.explanation: The name is a preference; the check guards against real harm. Insistence tells you nothing about which is which.
items.reference:
Principle or preference?
principle: crossing it changes what you will tolerate
preference: how you would rather things go
feeling strong tells you neither way
Why: the filter is what is actually at stake, because annoyance and a real principle feel equally strong.
items.learnMore:
A filter, not a feeling

Strong feelings come from ego as easily as from values. Asking what crossing the line would actually change is what separates the two.

Common mistake

Calling a preference a principle, so the label stops filtering anything.
items.reflection: Think of the last thing at work that really bothered you. If you ask what crossing it would change about what you tolerate, was it a principle or a preference?

items.prompt: Dana is furious when her proposal loses to a sound alternative, and calm when credit for a teammate's work is quietly taken. What does the unit suggest?
choices: Her feelings are accurate: anger marks real principles
Her calm shows she has no principles at all left
Her feelings are a poor guide: the first is likely ego
Both reactions show healthy, well-calibrated priorities
items.explanation: Feeling strength does not track stakes. The loud reaction may be ego while the quiet one points to something she should not tolerate.

preference: how you would rather things go

items.prompt: Someone says 'I only fight on principle' but objects to nearly every decision they disagree with. What is the likeliest problem?
choices: They have too many principles to ever satisfy
They are right about each one and should keep going
They fight too rarely for anyone to notice them
They label preferences as principles, so the label filters nothing
items.explanation: If everything is a principle, the word no longer separates the two, and credibility drains.

items.prompt: What is identity drift?
choices: A slow slide from skill-for-values to skill-for-itself
A single decision to trade your values for a promotion
Forgetting how to read a room after a long break
items.explanation: Drift is gradual and cumulative, not one dramatic choice.

items.prompt: Why is drift hard to catch?
choices: It only affects people who have weak values to begin with
Each step looks defensible and no moment feels wrong
It is always announced by one major, obvious event
items.explanation: Because every step passes a local test, no alarm goes off.

items.prompt: Which is harder to notice from inside?
choices: One big betrayal
They are equally easy to notice
Many small compromises
items.explanation: A big betrayal is visible; a series of small ones is not.

items.prompt: In the unit's teaching model, how does distance from your values grow?
choices: Slowly at first, then faster each month
Fast at first, then it levels off
By the same amount every single month
items.explanation: The curve starts gentle and steepens as compromises get easier.

items.prompt: What did Dana's four items have in common?
choices: Each was a clear breach of company policy when it happened
Each was done at the direct request of her manager
Each seemed fine alone; only the row of four looked off
items.explanation: The pattern was only visible once the items were lined up.

items.prompt: 'I can justify every single choice' is...
choices: Necessary, but also what someone mid-drift would say
Sufficient proof that no drift has happened over the months
A sign she should stop reviewing her choices
items.explanation: Local justification does not show the pattern is fine.

items.prompt: What makes the next compromise easier?
choices: A change in how performance is reviewed
The previous one passed without any alarm
The company having more people on the team
items.explanation: Each easy pass lowers the effective bar for the next.

items.prompt: Which is the better test for drift?
choices: Ask whether you can justify your most recent choice
Wait for a colleague to confront you
Line up months of actual small choices
items.explanation: The pattern across months is the signal, not the latest choice.

items.prompt: In the unit's teaching model, drift is 6% at month 4 and 42% at month 14. How should Dana read the early number?
choices: Safe, since a figure that low cannot grow into anything large
Small now, but the curve steepens; early quiet is no comfort
Misleading, since the curve is flat the whole way
Alarming, since it already proves she betrayed herself
items.explanation: The curve accelerates, so a low early value says little about where it goes.
items.reference:
Why drift hides
each step: individually defensible
no single moment feels wrong
the pattern shows only across months
Why: a hundred small, defensible compromises reach the same place as one betrayal, with no moment that felt like the wrong one.
items.learnMore:
Slow is the danger

A single betrayal can be named. Slow drift cannot, because every step passes the local test, so the test needs to be run on the whole stretch of months.

Common mistake

Checking only whether the latest choice was defensible.
items.reflection: Pick something you do now that you would have found odd two years ago. Was there a single moment it changed, or a series of small steps?

items.prompt: A friend says 'every political choice I made was reasonable, so I haven't drifted.' Which reply is strongest?
choices: You are right, since every one of your choices was reasonable
You should list only the principles you hold today
Each step passing is expected; check the pattern instead
You need one dramatic choice before it counts as drift
items.explanation: Per-choice justification is what drift looks like from inside; the pattern across months is what to check.

items.prompt: Which situation best fits identity drift rather than a single lapse?
choices: Many defensible choices over months end up somewhere nobody chose
One loud argument in which someone says something regrettable
A new job where norms differ and the person adapts openly
A deliberate decision to trade values for a promotion
items.explanation: Drift is cumulative and unnoticed. The others are a single event or a visible choice.

items.prompt: What are the three questions, in order?
choices: Who objects, how loudly they do, and how senior they are
Principle or preference, cost of losing, reversibility
Is it urgent, is it popular, is it cheap to fix
items.explanation: The order is principle, cost, reversibility.

items.prompt: Which question asks whether something can be undone later?
choices: Reversibility
Cost of losing
Principle or preference
items.explanation: Reversibility is the third question.

items.prompt: A battle worth having usually scores...
choices: Low on principle and cost but high on how it feels
High only on how strongly you feel about it
High on principle, cost, and irreversibility
items.explanation: Real principle, real cost, hard to undo.

items.prompt: A battle not worth having usually scores low on...
choices: Only the feeling of urgency
At least two of the three questions
None of the three questions at all
items.explanation: Low on two or more means it is not worth the capital.

items.prompt: Pure preference, tiny cost, fully reversible. What do you do?
choices: Yield and move on
Fight hard to set a precedent
Escalate it to the director
items.explanation: All three questions say it is not worth capital.

items.prompt: In the unit's model, what do repeated low-stakes fights do to credibility?
choices: Build it up through steady, repeated practice
Shrink what is left for the one that matters
Leave it exactly where it stood before them
items.explanation: Credibility remaining falls as the number of fights rises.

items.prompt: Two disagreements look identical. What tells them apart?
choices: Who raised each of them
Which meeting each came up in
What is actually at stake in each
items.explanation: Only the stakes differ; the surface does not.

items.prompt: What does 'cost of losing' mean here?
choices: The concrete cost that follows, not the sting
How embarrassed you would feel in the room that day
How long the meeting would run afterwards
items.explanation: It asks what actually happens because of the outcome.

items.prompt: One colleague's design silently drops error handling on a payment path. Another wants a different naming convention. How do the questions treat them?
choices: Both score the same way, since each is simply a disagreement in review
Naming scores higher, since more people see names every day
Design scores lower, since a shipped bug can be patched later
Design: principle, real cost, hard to undo; naming: the reverse
items.explanation: The design fails all three tests of 'yield'; the name fails them all the other way.
items.reference:
Three questions, in order
1. principle or preference?
2. is the cost of losing real and concrete?
3. can it be reversed later?
Why: a battle worth having is a real principle with a real cost that is hard to undo; low on two or more means yield.
items.learnMore:
Same surface, different stakes

Two disagreements can look identical in a meeting. Only checking what is at stake, the cost, and the reversibility tells you which one you are in.

Common mistake

Judging a battle by how it looks instead of by what it costs to lose.
items.reflection: Take a disagreement you are in right now and run the three questions in order. Where does it score low?

items.prompt: Principle: yes. Cost of losing: real. Reversible: easily, next quarter. What fits?
choices: Fight with everything, since principles always win out
Say your piece once, then let it go
Stay silent, since it can be fixed later anyway
Escalate immediately so the objection is on record
items.explanation: Real principle and cost justify speaking up, but easy reversal means no further capital.

items.prompt: A teammate fights every disagreement and is surprised when an objection about a real safety gap is waved off. Which explanation fits?
choices: The safety gap was not important enough to matter
Constant small fights spent the credibility the real one needed
The team dislikes the teammate for unrelated reasons
The objection should have been made louder than usual
items.explanation: Credibility is a shared budget; low-stakes fights draw it down before the one that counts.

items.prompt: How does the bar move?
choices: Management changes a rule in a single memo
One big decision lowers it all at once
Each easy pass makes the next one easier
items.explanation: The loosening is cumulative, not decided.

items.prompt: What replaces a decision once a compromise becomes routine?
choices: A habit, which is not re-examined
A policy, which is reviewed each year
A debate, which the team settles together
items.explanation: Habits skip the weighing a decision gets.

items.prompt: In step one, why is the skill built?
choices: The person wanted a faster climb up the career ladder
Not having it was genuinely costing the person
The company required it of everyone
items.explanation: It starts as a real response to a real cost.

items.prompt: As drift proceeds, the skill gets applied to...
choices: Larger and larger stakes
Mostly purely technical choices
Smaller and smaller stakes
items.explanation: Small stakes clear the low bar, so alarms stay quiet.

items.prompt: What is the signal worth looking for?
choices: One single choice that you came to regret later on
A gap between stated principles and actual choices
A colleague who openly disagrees with several choices
items.explanation: The gap between the two lists is the signal.

items.prompt: Which list should you compare with your principles?
choices: The actual small choices from recent months
The principles you would state if asked
The goals written in last year's review
items.explanation: Actual choices show what you do; stated principles show what you say.

items.prompt: Why are many small compromises hard to spot?
choices: They are always done in secret from the team
Each is far more harmful than a single big one
No single moment ever felt like the wrong one
items.explanation: There is no marked crossing point.

items.prompt: Which statement best captures the skill's role?
choices: The skill itself is the problem, so avoid building it
The skill is neutral; drift is in how it is used
Drift only happens to people who lack the skill
items.explanation: Dana still believes the skill is necessary.

items.prompt: Step 2 says the skill is applied to smaller stakes; step 3 says the bar itself moves. Which observation shows step 3?
choices: She applies the three questions to a much smaller issue than before
She learns a new method for building alliances
She is invited to join a planning committee
She stops running the questions because the answer feels settled
items.explanation: Step 3 is the habit forming: the check itself stops being run. Applying it to smaller stakes is step 2.
items.reference:
How the bar moves
1. skill built for a real reason
2. applied to smaller and smaller stakes
3. the bar moves; habit replaces decision
4. the crossing has no marked moment
Why: each easy pass makes the next easier to wave through, and a habit is not re-examined the way a decision is.
items.learnMore:
From decision to habit

A compromise that began as a deliberate trade-off gets repeated until it stops being weighed at all. The three questions stop being run because the answer feels settled.

Common mistake

Believing a one-time resolution can undo what a long accumulation built.
items.reflection: Where in your own work has a deliberate trade-off turned into something you do without weighing it? When did it stop being a decision?

items.prompt: Someone says 'I reviewed each choice when I made it, so drift can't apply to me.' What does the mechanism say?
choices: Each review passes a loosening bar, yet the total shift grows
Reviewing every single choice does guarantee there was no drift
Only a review by someone outside can ever detect any drift
Drift appears only when someone skips reviews entirely
items.explanation: If the bar loosens with every pass, each review is weaker than the last, so all can pass while the total moves far.

choices: A single firm resolution to be more direct from now on
Avoiding every situation that calls for political skill
A recurring review of recent actual choices against stated principles
Asking one trusted friend if you are a good person
items.explanation: The mechanism is cumulative, so the fix is a recurring check on the pattern, not a one-off correction.

items.prompt: What is institutional toxicity?
choices: An environment that clashes with the values you hold
One person behaving badly in one meeting last week
A bad quarter with an unusually heavy workload for all
items.explanation: It is a property of the organization, not an incident.

items.prompt: The first checklist question asks...
choices: Would my manager agree with me about all of this?
Would anyone equally principled face this pressure?
Could I find a better title somewhere else this year?
items.explanation: If anyone in your seat would, the cause is structural.

items.prompt: One failed attempt to raise a concern is...
choices: A proven institutional pattern
A reason to leave right away
An incident
items.explanation: One failure alone is just an incident.

items.prompt: Which is closer to an institutional signal?
choices: Repeated concerns, from several people, that change nothing
A single concern that was declined once
A disagreement that was eventually settled in your favor by the team
items.explanation: Repetition across attempts and people is the signal.

items.prompt: Is the incident-versus-organization call a formula?
choices: Yes, simply count the signals
Yes, ask for your manager's rating
No, it is a judgment call
items.explanation: The checks give evidence, not a verdict.

items.prompt: What is the cost of leaving too early?
choices: Abandoning a fixable situation and the people in it
Staying in a corrosive place for years
Losing the ability to raise any concern
items.explanation: A fixable situation may have been worth staying for.

items.prompt: What is the cost of staying too long in a corrosive place?
choices: Nothing, since you can always leave later
Something real and personal
Only a lower performance rating
items.explanation: The cost lands on you, not just on the work.

items.prompt: 'Is winning coherent here?' asks whether...
choices: You can win the next argument in the design review
Your team's goals for the whole quarter will all be met
A plausible path exists for staying to change things
items.explanation: It asks about the environment changing, not about one win.

items.prompt: An engineer raised a concern; then two teammates raised it separately; each time the response was a polite nod. Which reading fits best?
choices: Closer to institutional: several people, several tries, no change
An incident, since a polite nod is not an actual refusal to act on it
A communication issue that better slides would fix
Proof the engineers should stop raising concerns
items.explanation: Repetition across people and attempts with nothing moving is the institutional signal.
items.reference:
Incident or organization?
same pressure for anyone in your seat?
raising it ever changed anything?
is winning a coherent goal here?
Why: one failure is an incident; a repeated pattern across people with nothing moving points at the organization, though it is a judgment call.
items.learnMore:
Judgment, not a formula

The three checks give evidence, not a verdict. Leaving too early abandons something fixable; staying too long in a corrosive place costs something real and personal.

Common mistake

Treating one bad incident as proof the whole organization is hopeless, or the reverse.
items.reflection: Think of a recurring frustration at work. Would someone else in your seat face it too, and has raising it ever changed anything?

items.prompt: An engineer's one objection was overruled in one review. Others in the same seat report no such trouble. Which reading fits?
choices: Clearly institutional, since the objection was overruled
Proof of a hostile director who targets objections
Likely an incident: no shared structural pressure shows in the evidence
A sign the engineer should leave as soon as possible
items.explanation: A single event, with no shared pressure for others in the seat, points at an incident.

items.prompt: Which statement shows 'winning is coherent' failing?
choices: She won this week's technical argument with a colleague
Her manager disagrees with her about one design choice
She is tired after a long release at the very end of the month
No plausible path exists for staying to change the incentives
items.explanation: The question is whether the environment can change, not whether she can win single arguments.

items.prompt: When did Dana run the three questions?
choices: After the design had already shipped
Before the review, not during it
Only after Owen objected to her
items.explanation: She prepared rather than reacted.

items.prompt: Where did she raise the concern?
choices: In the review itself, where the decision was being made
In a private message after the meeting ended
In a note sent to the director afterward
items.explanation: The decision was being made in that room.

items.prompt: How was the claim framed?
choices: As a general worry about overall quality
As a criticism of Owen's judgment
As a specific, checkable technical claim
items.explanation: Specific and falsifiable, not accusatory.

items.prompt: Owen pushed back. What did Dana do with her tone?
choices: Matched his firmness so she could hold her ground
Kept steady and walked through it step by step
Dropped the point to keep the peace
items.explanation: She did not escalate to match him.

items.prompt: What risk did she describe?
choices: Some customers charged twice under one failure sequence
A slow page load at the checkout step
A missing log line in the retry path
items.explanation: A double-charge under a specific sequence.

items.prompt: What did the team do once the sequence proved real?
choices: Cancelled the whole change outright
Added a guard before shipping
Shipped it and planned a later patch
items.explanation: The guard went in before shipping.

items.prompt: Why was Owen not embarrassed?
choices: Dana praised his design to everyone in the room first
She sent the concern only to his manager
It stayed a technical disagreement, in the room
items.explanation: No public correction of a past mistake occurred.

items.prompt: What would Dana's drifting habit have done instead?
choices: Let it ride and flag it later if it grew
Raised it louder than the situation needed
Escalated it straight to the director
items.explanation: The method caught the version of her that would stay quiet.

items.prompt: Why does 'I think this reopens the double-charge case we hit in Q1; can we walk through the sequence?' beat 'This feels risky to me'?
choices: It sounds more confident, so people defer to it
It is specific, so the room can verify it directly
It avoids naming any particular risk to the customers
It signals that Dana expects to be overruled
items.explanation: A concrete claim can be tested together. A feeling can only be argued about.
items.reference:
Dana's review, in order
before the review: run the three questions
in the review: a specific, checkable claim
under pushback: same tone, walk the sequence
result: a guard added before shipping
Why: raising a checkable claim in the room where the decision is made keeps it a technical disagreement rather than a public correction.
items.learnMore:
Where and how, not only whether

The three questions settle whether to push. The place, the framing, and the tone under pushback decide whether the push lands.

Common mistake

Raising a real concern privately after the decision, when only a public reversal can fix it.
items.reflection: Imagine a concern you should raise soon. What is the room where the decision is actually made, and what is the specific, checkable claim you would make there?

items.prompt: Suppose Dana had raised the same concern in a private message to Owen after the decision was made. What is the main cost?
choices: Nothing is lost, since Owen would fix it quietly anyway
The concern would be treated as stronger than in the room
A fix now needs a reversal of a decision made in public
Owen would be more embarrassed than in the review
items.explanation: Once the decision is made, correcting it means reopening it, which is exactly what the review avoided.

Dana's review, in order
before the review: run the three questions
in the review: a specific, checkable claim
under pushback: same tone, walk the sequence
result: a guard added before shipping
Why: raising a checkable claim in the room where the decision is made keeps it a technical disagreement rather than a public correction.

items.reflection: Imagine a concern you should raise soon. What is the room where the decision is actually made, and what is the specific, checkable claim you would make there?

items.prompt: Owen insists the sequence is too narrow to matter. Which next step fits Dana's approach?
choices: Walk through the sequence until the room can judge
Repeat the concern more forcefully until he concedes
Agree it is narrow and note the risk in the ticket
Ask the director to rule on it before the review ends
items.explanation: She keeps the tone level and lets the sequence settle it, since it is checkable.

in the review: a specific, checkable claim

items.learnMore:
Where and how, not only whether

The three questions settle whether to push. The place, the framing, and the tone under pushback decide whether the push lands.

Common mistake

Raising a real concern privately after the decision, when only a public reversal can fix it.

A repeated warning until they act on it

You are not inside their slow accumulation

They do not value your opinion much

Every other case must match hers in every single detail
New constraints stress different parts of the method

A case, not the whole territory
